name: Aconite Violet
lede: Aconite Violet is a dusty purple named for aconite, the poisonous monkshood plant, and catalogued by Robert Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: A poisonous flower's purple
sections.body:
The name comes from aconite, the genus *Aconitum*, also called monkshood or wolfsbane, whose hooded flowers run from blue to this dusty purple [1]. The plant is one of the more toxic in the garden, long used to poison arrow tips and wolf bait, but the color name borrows only its flower, not its danger [1].

Robert Ridgway listed it in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, plate XXXVII, hue 63″ [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives an earlier record, 1905, and the ISCC-NBS system filed it in 1955 under block 223, a moderate purple [2][3]. Nearby named purples include [[faded-purple]] and [[dusty-purple]], both within three units of it, with [[viola]] a more vivid cousin and [[grey-purple]] a duller one [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds Aconite Violet in only 5 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.02 percent, as photographed [4]. That makes it one of the rarer named purples in the collection [4]. The measurement is a computed color match on scanned canvases, not a pigment identification [4].

The color is not one modern paintings reach for either: its five matches span from the fifteenth century to the early twentieth, with no single painter or school favoring it [4].
